2. Plaintiff-respondent No. 1 instituted the aforesaid suit in the second Court of the Assistant Judge, Satkania, for permanent injunction alleging, inter alia, that the suit land measuring 3. 23 acres under R.S. Khatian No. 836 belonged to one Fazar Ali in Korfa right and the raiyati right thereof belonged to Emdad Ali. Fazar Ali got mortgaged the suit land to one Jebunnessa and Basharat Ali by a registered deed dated 23.7.1921 and inducted them into possession of the suit land. Emdad Ali filed a rent suit against the heirs of Fazar Ali and the kot-mortgagees and got decree on 28.7.1938. During the pendency of the rent suit widow of Fazar Ali on her own behalf and on behalf of some minor children of said Fazar Ali executed a yearly kabuliyat relationg to 1.61 acres out of the suit land on 29.6.1938 in favour of Nurddin, predecessor of the defendant-appellants. A case was filed before the Debt Settlement Board for releasing the said kot mortagage which was executed by said Fazar Ali. That case was pending even after the passing of the rent decree in favour of Emdad Ali. The rent decree could not be executed as it was stayed by the Debt Settlement Board. However, when the stay order was vacated, in the rent execution Case No.1225 of 1938 the tenancy was auction sold on 10.9.1956 and the predecessor of the plaintiff, one Abdul Latif purchased the same in auction and took delivery of possession on 5.1.1957 and also annulled the encumbrances under Section 167 of the Bengal Tenancy Act namely, the interest of said Nuruddin, predecessor of the appellants. The said Abdul Latif mutated his name and paid rent. 

 4. The defendant Nuruddin died during the pendency of the suit and his heirs contested the same by filing a written statement. Upon denying the plaintiffs allegation, they asserted that the heirs of Fazar Ali first gave verbal lease to Nuruddin in the year 1936, accepted nazar and rents and placed him into possession of 1.61 acres out of the disputed land. Thereafter, the heirs of Fazar Ali, i.e. wife Bakumjan for hereself and on behalf of some of her minor children granted registered patta dated 29.6.38 and dakhilas in vavour of Nuruddin. He was in possession of 1.60 acres on payment of rent and he got corrected the record of right under Section 50 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. Plaintiffs vendor Abdul Latif raised objection there but it was rejected. Plaintiffs vendor earlier instituted a suit, O.S. 235 of 1957, against Nuruddin for declaration of his title to the suit land which was dismissed on 2.7.1959. 

 5. The defendant's further case is that the wholesale acquisition of rent receiving interest took place on 14.4.1956 and Nuruddin became direct tenant under the Government on and from 14.4.1956 prior to the rent sale on 10.9.56 on due payment of rent to the Government from 1363 B.S.  (1956 to 1981). Therefore, the rent sale was nothing but a money sale. The defendants being direct tenants under the Government was not an encumbrance nor it was an annullable one. 

 11. It appears that both the trial Court and the learned judge of the High Court Division while dealing with the question of title totally failed to take notice of the relevant provisions of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act 1950, briefly the Act, pertaining to the provisions relating to arrear rents etc. and their realisation which accured prior to their vesting in the Government under Clause (C) of Sub-section (4) of section 3 or under Clause (7) of Section 44 of the Act. The learned Assistant Judge thoroughly misdirected himself in taking the view that the rent suit, execution proceeding etc. were to continue under the old law i.e. the Bengal Tenancy Act notwithstanding the promulgation of the Act in 1951. He observed that the sale in question could be held legally and validly under the old law by reason of Section 6 and 7 of the General Clauses Act. Having further found that there was a valid rent sale on 10.9.56 and Abdul Latif obtained delivery of possession from the judgment debtors, it was held that the plaintiffs title was genuine and true. 

 15. Then there came Ordinance No. III of 1956. The East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy (Amendment) Ordinance, 1956, which came into force on 22 March, 1956, adding a new Chapter, IXA, providing for "Special Provisions relating to arrears of rent." For our present purpose the provisions of Section 68B thereof only are relevant which read thus: 

 18. It has been noticed by the Courts below and we have also seen that so far as documentary evidence is concerned relationg to payment of rent, record of right etc. the case of both the parties seem to stand at par. One of the grievances made by the learned Advocate for the appellants, however, is that the defendants documents, namely, Ext. B. C, D, E, G and H series were not at all considered by the learned Judge of the High Court Division. That this grievance has substance cannot be denied inasmuch as no reference is to be found to the said documents in the impugned judgment of the High Court Division. It appears that of the defendants' documents, the learned Judge of the High Court Division only considered Ext. A, certified copy of the patta dated 29.6.38 and observed, inter alia, that the same was completely demolished by the notice of the auction-purchaser under Section 167 of the B.T. Act. In view of the relevant provision of law referred to above, it is hardly necessary to point out that the notice under Section 167 B.T. Act was merely an exercise in futility. The documents and papers relating to auction sale and delivery of possession could hardly be of any help to the plaintiff for proving his possession. In the same manner, the P.S. Khatian, the dakhilas, although evidence of possession could hardly advance his case of actual possession of the suit land for the simple reason that the defendants had as much khatian and dakhilas in their names as were sufficient to match those of the plaintiffs. Among the large number of documents filed by the defendants showing mutation and payment of rent by them, reference may be made to Ext. C(2) which is a copy of the order sheet of Misc. Case No. 344 of 1964 under Section 50 of the Act. It appears that at the instance of Nuruddin, predecessor of the defendants the Revenue Officer ordered that 8 annas of Plot No. 2110 (i.e. 1.61 acres) be transferred to his Khatian No. 1215. Ext.C(3), E, E(1) F consistently support the defendant's case in respect of their share claimed out of the suit land. Dakhilas Ext. B series and H series are there in support of the defendants' case. However, we do not think that such documents proved on either side were such upon which actual possession could be decided. The plaintiff was at a disadvantage with his documents relating to his title for the reasons already stated. It was incumbent upon him to prove actual possession, by adducing oral evidence sufficient enough to carry conviction firstly, by his vendor Abdul Latif and then by himself. It will be seen that in order to prove possession plaintiff only examined himself as P.W.1 and his brother-in-law Badi Ahmed, P.W.2 and nobody else, Defendants on their part also examined two witnesses. In the facts and circumstances of the case noticed above it must be said that the evidence adduced by the plaintiff was not only meagre but wholly unconvincing for the purpose of proving actual possession in the suit land. Indeed there was no independent and reiable evidence on the side of the plaintiff to support his case of possession. 

 20. So far as the impugned judgment of the High Court Division is concerned, there is no consideration of any oral evidence except saying that the trial Court has believed the evidence of possession by the P.Ws. The learned Judge of the High Court Division failed to consider that in the facts and circumstances of the case the oral evidence of possession as adduced by the plaintiff was utterly inadequate, skimpy and just not legally sufficient for granting a decree of permanent injunction. We have no manner of doubt that had the learned Judge of the High Court Division been aware of the legal provisions referred to above which under the documents (relating to rent sale etc.) relied upon and proved by the plaintiff to be of little value as far as possession is concerned and further if it was noticed that except that of the plaintiff and his brother-in-law there was no independent evidence of possession, the suit could not have been decreed. We are clearly of the opinion that in the facts and circumstances of the case, the evidence adduced is plainly insufficient to sustain a decree for permanent injunction. For the reasons stated above the impugned judgment and decree cannot be allowed to stand.
